To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) Tregs can suppress the proliferation of T cells that are protected from apoptosis and necroptosis; 2) Tregs can induce the death of conventional T cells by necroptosis, but not by apoptosis; and 3) Tregs can inhibit the activation and proliferation of T cells by a mechanism that is independent of the programmed cell death pathways.

1) Tregs are able, in vitro and in a number of in vivo models, to suppress the proliferation and effector function of conventional T cells, even in the presence of resistance to apoptosis (Bcl-2, Bim, Puma) and regulated necrosis (Ripk-3).
Tregs are able not to suppress the proliferation or survival of conventional T cells, which are resistant to apoptosis and necroptosis.

the molecular mechanisms of regulatory T-cell function and their potential use in the treatment of inflammatory diseases.
the molecular basis of Treg function, with a particular focus on the role of programmed cell death pathways.
